The use of contrast-enhanced breast MRI during pregnancy is 
contraindicated because gadolinium in all forms crosses the placenta and 
enters the fetal circulation.259,261,262 There are concerns that the gadolinium 
ion may then dissociate in the fetal circulation and cause toxicity for the 
fetus. The exact frequency of this occurring and the associated impact of 
dissociated gadolinium on fetal toxicity is uncertain as there are no reliable 
data on fetal safety of gadolinium exposure during pregnancy. Therefore, 
gadolinium administered with breast MRI is best avoided during 
pregnancy, and other modes of breast imaging should be used. 
Non-contrast MRI is not recommended due to lack of sensitivity. 

manyfold below the threshold of fetal teratogenesis,260 due to the 
infrequency of PABC250 and the decreased sensitivity and specificity of 
mammography during pregnancy and lactation,253 providers and patients 
may implement a short delay in routine breast imaging based on date of 
delivery and/or prior imaging in individuals who are at average risk of 
breast cancer until after pregnancy and lactation. There are no data 
evaluating the use of ultrasound alone as an alternative screening method 
in individuals at average risk of breast cancer during pregnancy or 
lactation; therefore, it is not recommended as an alternative to screening 
mammography. Supplemental screening should be considered for 
individuals who are pregnant and lactating who have heterogenous or 
extremely dense breasts and are at average risk of breast cancer. 

Screening in Individuals at Increased Risk of Breast Cancer 
Recommendations for breast cancer screening in individuals at increased 
risk of developing breast cancer who are pregnant or lactating include 
CBE and age-appropriate mammogram with tomosynthesis. The use of 
screening ultrasound alone has not been evaluated as a method to reduce 
breast cancer mortality in individuals who are pregnant or lactating and are 
at increased risk for breast cancer. While contrast-enhanced MRI is not 
recommended during pregnancy due to the trans-placental passage of 
gadolinium,259,261,262 it is appropriate to recommend screening breast MRI 
at routine intervals for individuals at increased risk of developing breast 
cancer who are lactating given the minimal excretion of gadolinium into 
human breast milk.257,263,266 

It is recommended that individuals who are lactating either pump the 
breast or breastfeed just prior to imaging to improve sensitivity and 
comfort of the examination. Fortunately, there is minimal excretion of 
gadolinium into human breast milk, with <1% of permitted neonatal dose 
of contrast over the first 24 hours after maternal administration.263 Breast 
MRI appears to be highly sensitive for the detection of known PABC, 
although there appears to be lower specificity of breast MRI (higher 
false-positive rate) in individuals who undergo breast MRI while still 
lactating.264 If individuals undergo breast MRI, due to the minimal contrast 
excretion into breast milk, individuals are not required to “pump and 
discard” breast milk after administration.259 The ACR states that there is no 
role for molecular breast imaging (Tc-99m Sestamibi MBI) in breast cancer 
screening or evaluation of breast complaints during pregnancy or lactation 
and is in fact contraindicated in screening during pregnancy.261,265

Management of Breast Signs and Symptoms During Pregnancy and 
Lactation 

Palpable Symptom 
Age-appropriate evaluation of a palpable symptom during pregnancy or 
lactation should proceed similar to that for individuals who are not 
pregnant or lactating (see Palpable Symptom in the algorithm). If 

Screening in Individuals ≥40 Years at Average Risk of Breast Cancer 
Recommendations for breast cancer screening in individuals ≥40 years of 
age who are pregnant or lactating and who are at average risk for 
developing breast cancer include a CBE and mammogram with 
tomosynthesis. While ionizing radiation exposure with mammography is

should be consulted to discuss possible further diagnostic testing (eg, duct

Suspicious Skin Changes 
Individuals who are pregnant with suspicious skin changes should 
undergo age-appropriate breast imaging evaluation similar to that for 
individuals who are not pregnant or lactating, with diagnostic mammogram 
with tomosynthesis with or without ultrasound (see Skin Changes in the 
algorithm). If mammographic and/or ultrasound imaging is negative and 
findings are clinically suspicious, consider CEM or skin punch biopsy. 

Nipple Inversion/Retraction without Palpable Mass 
Age-appropriate evaluation of a palpable symptom during pregnancy or 
lactation should proceed similar to that for individuals who are not 
pregnant or lactating (see Nipple Inversion/Retraction without Palpable 
Mass in the algorithm). If mammographic and/or ultrasound imaging is 
negative and findings are clinically suspicious, consider CEM. Breast MRI 
is not contraindicated for the management of nipple inversion/retraction 
without palpable mass during lactation if clinically indicated. 

Suspicious skin changes in individuals who are lactating may be due to 
puerperal mastitis. If symptoms are clinically consistent with mastitis, 
appropriate treatment should proceed, including the use of antimicrobials. 
Mastitis that does not improve with usual treatment should result in both 
clinical and imaging evaluation for alternative etiologies (eg, breast 
abscess, breast cancer). Breast imaging is nearly always indicated to 
assist in the diagnosis of persistent breast skin changes that have not 
responded to usual treatment for mastitis. In this circumstance, 
age-appropriate evaluation should proceed similar to that for individuals 
who are not lactating (see Skin Changes in the algorithm). 

Breast ultrasound is particularly useful in diagnosing breast abscess and 
may be the appropriate first imaging modality. If breast abscess is found, 
drainage is usually indicated and provides a definitive diagnosis. 

Nipple Discharge, No Palpable Symptom 
Because of the frequency of normal nipple discharge during pregnancy 
and lactation, the NCCN Panel defines abnormal nipple discharge as 
spontaneous, uniductal, unilateral bloody or clear nipple discharge that is 
persistent and reproducible on exam. Due to normal physiologic changes 
of pregnancy and lactation, bloody nipple discharge is common, but 
usually short-lived.267,268 Persistence beyond one or two episodes should 
undergo evaluation. Spontaneous multi-duct discharge that is milky may 
be due to pregnancy, and if not, should be evaluated for galactorrhea. 
Greenish, coffee-colored, yellow, brown/black multi-duct discharge is 
nearly always non-neoplastic, and reassurance can be provided. However, 
if the discharge is bothersome to the patient, referral to a breast specialist 
may be considered. Age-appropriate evaluation of abnormal nipple 
discharge during lactation should proceed similar to that for individuals 
who are not pregnant or lactating (See Nipple Discharge, No Palpable 
Symptom in the algorithm). If mammographic and/or ultrasound imaging is 
negative and findings are clinically suspicious, consider CEM. Breast MRI 
is not contraindicated for the management of abnormal nipple discharge 
during lactation if clinically indicated. If there is persistent bloody nipple 
discharge without abnormal breast imaging, a breast surgical expert 

Persistent or Severe Focal Breast Pain 
While breast pain is common due to the physiologic changes of pregnancy 
and lactation and is considered normal, individuals with focal persistent 
breast pain (defined as lasting 4–6 weeks in duration) should undergo 
age-appropriate evaluation as outlined for those who are not pregnant or 
lactating (see Persistent or Severe Breast Pain in the algorithm). If 
mammographic and/or ultrasound imaging is negative and findings are

clinically suspicious, consider CEM or palpable biopsy. While breast MRI 
is not contraindicated for the management of persistent, focal breast pain 
during lactation, it is usually not indicated. 

Summary 

The intent of the NCCN Guidelines for Breast Cancer Screening and 
Diagnosis is to give clinicians a practical, consistent framework for 
screening and evaluating a spectrum of clinical breast presentations. 
Clinical judgment should always be an important component of the optimal 
management of the patient. 
 

Axillary Mass(es) Suspected to Represent Adenopathy 
The development of an axillary mass during pregnancy may be due to 
normal breast enlargement that occurs during pregnancy or lactation in 
accessory axillary breast tissue that is present in ~15% of individuals. It is 
also not uncommon for this to be asymmetric. The development of an 
axillary mass within the first 2 weeks following delivery is clinically 
consistent with lactational changes due to the presence of axillary breast 
tissue. 

If after clinical examination there remains concern that the physical 
findings are not due to normal axillary breast tissue that has enlarged due 
to pregnancy, providers should proceed with evaluation as outlined for 
individuals who are not pregnant or lactating (See Axillary Mass in the 
algorithm). If suspicious axillary lymph nodes are identified, 
mammography is recommended. 

BI-RADS Category Imaging Follow-up 
Pregnancy or lactation should not change the management of follow-up of 
a BI-RADS 3 imaging finding, and appropriate follow-up imaging and/or 
examination should proceed as outlined for individuals who are not 
pregnant or lactating (see Mammographic and/or Ultrasound Evaluation 
and Follow-up in the algorithm). In the case of a BI-RADS 3 finding on MRI 
without associated ultrasound or mammography findings in an individual 
who is pregnant, a breast expert should be consulted to assist with 
counseling regarding follow-up and management recommendations (eg, 
defer to after pregnancy). 

Because it is rare to develop a milk fistula after core needle biopsy,269

Table 1: Breast Cysts - Types and Definitions 

 

 

Simple 

Anechoic (cystic), well-circumscribed, 
round, or oval with well-defined 
imperceptible wall and posterior 
enhancement. 

 
 

Complicated 
Has most but not all elements of a simple 
cyst. Complicated cysts do not contain 
solid elements, intracystic masses, thick 
walls, or thick septa. This type of cyst may 
contain low-level echoes or intracystic 
debris, and can be described as a round, 
circumscribed mass containing low-level 
echoes without vascular flow, fulfilling 
most but not all criteria of a simple cyst. 

Complex 
Has some discrete solid component, 
which may include thick walls, thick septa, 
and/or intracystic mass. Complex cysts 
have both anechoic (cystic) and echogenic 
(solid) components.

nodes.text: SCREENING/FOLLOW-UP • Clinical encounter every 1–3 y • Breast awareness

footnotes.text: Breast Screening Considerations (BSCR-A).

At minimum, medical and family history should be reviewed and clinical encounter should encompass ongoing risk assessment (by age 25 years), risk reduction counseling, and preferably a clinical breast examination (CBE) even in individuals who are asymptomatic when feasible. Known breast density should be factored into risk assessment if available from a prior mammogram.

Rationale for recommending clinical encounter is to maximize earliest detection of breast cancers and assure ongoing risk assessment, particularly in regions where mammographic screening may not be accessible. Randomized trials comparing incremental CBE versus mammographic screening have not been performed.
Individuals should be familiar with their breasts and promptly report changes to their health care provider. See Signs/Symptoms During Clinical Encounter (BSCR-5).

Medicare and insurers allow the individual direct access to scheduling for screening mammography.

At minimum, medical and family history should be reviewed and clinical encounter should encompass ongoing risk assessment (by age 25 years), risk reduction counseling, and preferably a clinical breast examination (CBE) even in individuals who are asymptomatic when feasible. Known breast density should be factored into risk assessment if available from a prior mammogram.

Rationale for recommending clinical encounter is to maximize earliest detection of breast cancers and assure ongoing risk assessment, particularly in regions where mammographic screening may not be accessible. Randomized trials comparing incremental CBE versus mammographic screening have not been performed.
Individuals should be familiar with their breasts and promptly report changes to their health care provider. See Signs/Symptoms During Clinical Encounter (BSCR-5).
See Mammographic and/or ultrasound evaluation (BSCR-18).
Shared decision-making is encouraged based on individuals' values and preferences.
Tomosynthesis can decrease call-back rates and improve cancer detection compared with two-dimensional (2D) mammography alone.

In patients with extremely dense breasts and normal mammograms, supplemental screening with breast MRI decreases interval cancers. In a prospective study, those randomized to breast MRI after a negative screening mammogram had significantly fewer interval breast cancers compared to those who did not have supplemental screening (category 1 for ages 50–75 y). The ideal frequency of supplemental screening MRI in this patient population is not yet known. See Discussion.

footnotes.text: Breast Screening Considerations (BSCR-A).
Medicare and insurers allow the individual direct access to scheduling for screening mammography.

At minimum, medical and family history should be reviewed and clinical encounter should encompass ongoing risk assessment (by age 25 years), risk reduction counseling, and preferably a CBE even in individuals who are asymptomatic when feasible. Known breast density should be factored into risk assessment if available from a prior mammogram.

Rationale for recommending clinical encounter is to maximize earliest detection of breast cancers and assure ongoing risk assessment, particularly in regions where mammographic screening may not be accessible. Randomized trials comparing incremental CBE versus mammographic screening have not been performed. (BSCR-5).
Individuals should be familiar with their breasts and promptly report changes to their health care provider. See Signs/Symptoms During Clinical Encounter (BSCR-5).
See Mammographic and/or ultrasound evaluation (BSCR-18).
Tomosynthesis can decrease call-back rates and improve cancer detection compared with 2D mammography alone.
Including first-, second-, and, when included in the model, third-degree relatives.
Consider mammogram beginning at age 25 years on a case-by-case basis depending on family history or for patients who cannot undergo breast MRI.

High-quality breast MRI requires a dedicated breast coil, access to biopsy under MRI guidance, experienced radiologists in breast MRI, and regional availability. MRI should be correlated with other breast imaging modalities.

Many experts recommend alternating the mammogram and breast MRI with and without contrast every 6 months. While there are limited data to support this approach, the presumption is that this may lead to earlier identification of cancer.
Except in rare circumstances of a family history of very-early-onset breast cancers before age 30 years.
Of note, some individuals at increased risk of breast cancer may undergo breast MRI prior to qualifying for screening mammogram.
In a recent direct comparison trial, MRI had a cancer detection rate (CDR) approximately 4 times higher than ultrasound in patients with dense breasts. See Discussion.

Medicare and insurers allow the individual direct access to scheduling for screening mammography.

At minimum, medical and family history should be reviewed and clinical encounter should encompass ongoing risk assessment (by age 25 years), risk reduction counseling, and preferably a CBE even in individuals who are asymptomatic when feasible. Known breast density should be factored into risk assessment if available from a prior mammogram.

Rationale for recommending clinical encounter is to maximize earliest detection of breast cancers and assure ongoing risk assessment, particularly in regions where mammographic screening may not be accessible. Randomized trials comparing incremental CBE versus mammographic screening have not been performed.
Individuals should be familiar with their breasts and promptly report changes to their health care provider. See Signs/Symptoms During Clinical Encounter (BSCR-5).
See Mammographic and/or ultrasound evaluation (BSCR-18).
Tomosynthesis can decrease call-back rates and improve cancer detection compared with 2D mammography alone.

In patients with extremely dense breasts and normal mammograms, supplemental screening with breast MRI decreases interval cancers. In a prospective study, those randomized to breast MRI after a negative screening mammogram had significantly fewer interval breast cancers compared to those who did not have supplemental screening (category 1 for ages 50–75 y). See Discussion. The ideal frequency of supplemental screening MRI in this patient population is not yet known.

High-quality breast MRI requires a dedicated breast coil, access to biopsy under MRI guidance, experienced radiologists in breast MRI, and regional availability. MRI should be correlated with other breast imaging modalities.

Many experts recommend alternating the mammogram and breast MRI with and without contrast every 6 months. While there are limited data to support this approach, the presumption is that this may lead to earlier identification of cancer.

Including mass, new-onset asymmetric thickening/nodularity, asymmetric breast enlargement, or change in shape/contour (which may be due to implant rupture). See https://www.fda.gov/media/131885/download and BSCR-6.

nodes.text: Acquired/new-onset nipple inversion/retraction without palpable mass

footnotes.text: For management of signs/symptoms in individuals AMAB, see BSCR-14.

For individuals with signs and symptoms, clinical encounter should include, at a minimum, a review of medical and family history, and CBE. Subsequent visits should include risk assessment (by age 25 years) and risk reduction counseling. Known breast density should be factored into risk assessment if available from a prior mammogram.

Individuals with breast implants have a very small risk of developing breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL) (average 7–9 years after implantation) and breast implant-associated squamous cell carcinoma (BIA-SCC). The majority of cases of BIA-ALCL have been seen in textured implants, while BIA- SCC is associated with either smooth or textured implants. For breast-implant–related symptoms occurring >1 year post-implantation that are concerning for BIA-ALCL (effusion, enlargement, mass) or BIA-SCC (ulceration), consultation with a multidisciplinary team with experience in managing these disorders is recommended. For BIA-ALCL, also see NCCN Guidelines for T-Cell Lymphomas.

Attention to timely diagnostic follow-up after abnormal breast screening is recommended, as racial disparities have been observed in time to diagnostic imaging and/or biopsy following abnormal breast screening. See Discussion.

age_years.definition: Patient age in years at the encounter.

chest_rt_breast_exposure.definition: Patient received radiation therapy (RT) with exposure of breast tissue (e.g. chest or mantle field).

chest_rt_age_years.definition: Patient age in years when the breast-tissue-exposing RT was given. Unset if no such RT.

residual_lifetime_breast_cancer_risk_per.definition: Residual lifetime breast cancer risk from a model that includes a comprehensive family history.

five_year_risk_gail_percent.definition: 5-year risk of invasive breast cancer calculated by the Gail model.

five_year_risk_imaging_model_percent.definition: 5-year risk of invasive breast cancer calculated by an imaging-based risk assessment model.

pedigree_genetic_predisposition.definition: Family pedigree is suggestive of, or the patient has a known, genetic predisposition to breast cancer.

prior_adh_or_lobular_neoplasia.definition: Prior pathology shows atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) or lobular neoplasia (LCIS or ALH).

prior_breast_cancer_history.definition: Patient has a prior history of breast cancer.

palpable_breast_symptom.definition: A palpable breast symptom or mass is present on history or examination.

palpable_symptom_not_explained_by_gyneco.definition: A palpable breast symptom is present that is not explained by gynecomastia.

palpable_symptom_persists_after_observat.definition: The palpable symptom is still present on re-examination after 1-2 menstrual cycles of observation.

axillary_mass_present.definition: One or more axillary masses are present that are suspected to represent adenopathy.

axillary_mass_laterality.definition: Side(s) on which the axillary mass or masses are found.

axillary_node_biopsy_result.definition: Pathology result of axillary lymph node sampling, with origin of any malignancy.

nipple_retraction_status.definition: Nipple inversion or retraction without palpable mass: acquired/new onset, or congenital/life-long.

nipple_inversion_recent_change.definition: Recent change in a congenital or life-long nipple inversion.

nipple_discharge_single_duct_unilateral.definition: Nipple discharge comes from a single duct on one breast.

nipple_discharge_appearance.definition: Colour or nature of the nipple discharge.

nipple_discharge_persistent_reproducible.definition: Nipple discharge is persistent and reproducible on examination.

skin_peau_d_orange.definition: Peau d'orange (pitted or dimpled skin) is present.

skin_scaling_or_eczema.definition: Skin scaling or eczema is present.

breast_pain_present.definition: Breast pain of any kind is reported.

breast_pain_persistent_or_severe.definition: Breast pain is persistent or severe.

breast_pain_pattern.definition: Pattern of breast pain on examination.

systemic_disease_present.definition: Systemic disease is present on clinical evaluation.

bilateral_breast_enlargement.definition: Bilateral breast enlargement consistent with gynecomastia or pseudogynecomastia is present.

clinically_suspicious.definition: Clinician judgement of clinical suspicion for malignancy after history and examination.

clinical_exam_abnormal.definition: Clinical breast examination findings are abnormal.

birads_category.definition: BI-RADS category from the most recent mammographic and/or ultrasound evaluation.

imaging_pathology_concordance.definition: Whether the pathology result is concordant with the imaging findings.

biopsy_pathology.definition: Pathology result of core needle biopsy or surgical excision.

follow_up_change.definition: Change in a previously found finding on follow-up physical examination or imaging.

aspiration_outcome.definition: Outcome of fine-needle aspiration of a mass.

clinician_elects_duct_excision.definition: Clinician judgement that duct excision is chosen over continued follow-up for a nipple discharge finding.

symptom_present.definition: Any breast sign or symptom is present.

skin_change_present.definition: Any listed skin change is present.

skin_change_listed_findings.definition: Any of the skin changes listed in the skin-changes box: peau d'orange, edema, erythema, nipple excoriation, scaling or eczema, skin ulceration. Excludes skin thickening and skin discoloration, which the box does not list.

inflammatory_breast_cancer_suspicion.definition: Skin findings that raise suspicion for possible inflammatory breast cancer.

paget_or_other_breast_skin_suspicion.definition: Skin findings that raise suspicion for Paget disease or other manifestations of breast cancer.

angiosarcoma_suspicion.definition: Skin findings that raise suspicion for angiosarcoma.

nipple_discharge_non_spontaneous_or_mult.definition: Nipple discharge that is non-spontaneous or from multiple ducts.

spontaneous_single_duct_discharge.definition: Spontaneous, unilateral, single-duct, clear or bloody discharge that is persistent and reproducible on examination.

residual_lifetime_risk_ge_20.definition: Residual lifetime breast cancer risk is 20 percent or more.

chest_rt_window_10_to_30.definition: Breast-tissue-exposing RT given between ages 10 and 30 years.

gail_risk_criterion.definition: Gail 5-year risk is 1.7 percent or more in an individual aged 35 years or older.

imaging_risk_criterion.definition: 5-year risk of invasive breast cancer by an imaging-based model is 1.7 percent or more.

dense_breast_criterion.definition: Heterogeneously or extremely dense breasts on mammography.

increased_risk.definition: Patient meets at least one increased risk criterion.

risk_category.definition: Breast cancer risk category for screening.

history_and_physical_finding.definition: Dominant finding on history and physical examination.

clinical_or_mri_abnormal.definition: Clinical findings or MRI findings are abnormal (MRI BI-RADS 4 or 5).

axillary_node_disposition.definition: Next step for axillary lymph node sampling result. Mapping of the three listed child boxes to the four parent results is inferred from box order.

follow_up_stable.definition: Follow-up shows stable, decreased, resolved or now definitively benign findings.

follow_up_significant_increase.definition: Follow-up shows a significant increase in size or increased suspicion.

aspiration_bloody_nontraumatic.definition: Mass resolved with non-traumatic bloody fluid obtained on aspiration.

gynecomastia_workup_trigger.definition: Palpable symptom not explained by gynecomastia, or bloody nipple discharge.

notes.predicates: Conditions were drafted and reviewed by a language model (model_reviewed), not by clinicians. 'rejected' means the review rejected the draft; the box then needs clinician judgement. 'section_only' means the box only requires the patient to be in the page's guideline section.
notes.coordinates: bbox and line_bboxes are PDF points with the origin at the page's top left; pages[].size gives the page size.
notes.links: page links name a page id from pages[]; a multi-page code such as PROS-F has ids 'PROS-F 1 of 5' ... ; external_guideline links name another guideline's slug.
